extracted.intended_audience: regulatory lawyers, policy makers, CRTC staff, broadcasters/telecommunications stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, legal principles, and recommended safeguards governing CRTC hearings, Cabinet/ministerial directions and appeals, public disclosure and natural justice in broadcasting and telecommunications regulation in Canada.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards for direction powers (publication and consultative requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directives should be public, tabled in Parliament, published in the Canada Gazette, and not pertain to specific individual cases but to broad policy matters. There should be an opportunity for both the agency and the public to be consulted prior to the issuance of a directive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report endorses requirement that all directives be public, tabled in Parliament and published; recommends referral of proposed directions to the agency which may request public submissions and must make a public report within 90 days (or further specified period) so the exercise of direction is exposed to scrutiny before becoming final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to direction power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cabinet's direction power (in proposed telecommunications legislation) should not extend to: (1) issuance/amendment/renewal of a broadcasting licence to a particular applicant; (2) the content of programming; (3) the application of qualitative standards to programming; (4) the restriction of freedom of expression; (5) charges to be levied for particular telecommunications services or the revenue requirements of a particular telecommunications carrier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five exceptions were listed as limits on direction power to protect core adjudicative/licensing and free-expression matters from political interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to retain limited review/remedy where direction is ignored or misapplied
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a direction power exists, a limited right to set aside decisions should be retained where the agency has ignored or misapplied a direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper supports abolishing Cabinet appeals where a direction power exists but recommends retaining a limited right for Cabinet to set aside decisions if agency ignores/misapplies a direction; Cabinet should act on its own motion or petition of an interested party but must give notice and an opportunity to respond in writing before a final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and opportunity to respond before Cabinet acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of the Cabinet's intention to act, or of any petition received by it, should be given to all interested parties and the CRTC with a full opportunity for all to respond in writing before the Cabinet makes a final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation intended to reduce secrecy/after-the-fact interference and to preserve credibility of CRTC procedures by ensuring affected parties can comment before Cabinet intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a 'stop order' for matters raising significant policy implications
rubrics_metrics.description: A mechanism such as a 'stop order' could halt proceedings until Cabinet has had an opportunity to decide whether a direction was necessary when an application raises major policy implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such mechanisms require Cabinet to act early and for the CRTC to keep the Minister informed of applications likely to raise significant policy questions; Cabinet might also convert adjudicatory proceedings into advisory ones where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministerial appeals should be open with notice to interveners
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministerial appeals (e.g., special appeal process for CBC matters) should be conducted in the open with notice of and an opportunity to comment on submissions made to the Minister provided to interveners who participated in the licensing hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current private conduct of ministerial appeals can introduce considerations not publicly aired and undermine credibility; open process with notice is recommended to address those objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate notice by the Commission of its concerns on licence renewal applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRTC should, in its notices, spell out any concerns that may lead it to fail to renew or revoke a licence so parties know the reasons they are being asked to appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confederation Broadcasting case highlighted inadequate notice; since then the Commission has taken care to indicate serious concerns prior to calling a licensee to hearing. Adequate notice is 'particularly critical for licensees whose licences may be in jeopardy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disclosure of application material / limits on confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: While applicants may request confidentiality for certain kinds of information under Rule 20, public hearings should provide members of the public with reasonable opportunity to know the subject matter of the hearing, including access to application materials where required for a 'public hearing' under the Broadcasting Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re: London Cable case — denying public access to financial documents was held inconsistent with requirement of a public hearing; Chief Justice Jackett described a public hearing as one where 'every member of the public would have a status to bring before the Commission anything relevant' and have 'sufficient time' to prepare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion to convene public hearings (and limits of judicial review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for new licences and cases involving possible suspension or revocation, the CRTC has discretion whether to hold a public hearing; courts may only review whether the CRTC actually exercised that discretion, not substitute their own view of the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National Indian Brotherhood v. Juneau (No. 3) held judicial review limited to whether the CRTC put its mind to whether a hearing was in the public interest; courts should not substitute discretion for that of the regulator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing applications at time of licence renewal or transfer (duty to hear)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate whether the CRTC has a legal duty to hear competing applications at renewal/transfer; the Federal Court of Appeal ruled the CRTC is under no legal duty to hear competing applications for renewals, though some trial-level decisions have found a duty in the interests of natural justice and the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capital Cable litigation: trial judge ordered hearing of competing application to assist CRTC's public interest objectives; Court of Appeal later found no legal duty, illustrating tension between legal duty and policy arguments for competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meetings between Commissioners and potential applicants — record-keeping and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When Commissioners meet privately with licensees or representatives about matters that may become the subject of an application, detailed minutes should be kept and made part of the public record to avoid charges of potential bias or failure to disclose relevant information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private continuous meetings help regulation, but where topics could be subject of future applications, lack of a public record makes agency vulnerable to bias/natural justice claims (illustrated in Canadian Broadcasting League v. CRTC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between investigatory/administrative meetings and adjudicative consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction exists between exploratory/investigatory meetings to ascertain facts for the purpose of deciding whether to convene a hearing (administrative, not subject to natural justice) and consideration of issues to which those facts give rise (adjudicative, subject to natural justice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have treated fact-finding/preliminary meetings as administrative; natural justice rules apply once matters move into adjudicative decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public hearing procedures should enable meaningful participation (timely notice, opportunity to prepare)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public hearings must be arranged to provide members of the public with reasonable opportunity to know the subject matter of the hearing in sufficient time to decide whether to participate and to prepare representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Justice Jackett's formulation: hearings should allow public to bring anything relevant and have sufficient time to exercise statutory right of presentation and prepare; procedural rules and Commission's inherent jurisdiction apply subject to this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telecommunications proceedings — more formal procedures reduce natural justice appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Telecommunications decisions since acquisition of jurisdiction have seen fewer natural justice appeals, perhaps reflecting more formal procedures in that area; challengers have often sought Cabinet petitions rather than judicial appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 1976–1979 there were only a few appeals of telecommunications decisions, and they centered on substantive law rather than procedural fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review timeframe and scope (Federal Court of Appeal jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Court of Appeal exercises appellate jurisdiction over broadcasting and telecommunications decisions of the CRTC; an appeal lies on a question of law or jurisdiction upon leave being obtained within one month of the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because CRTC powers are broad and discretionary, appellate review offers limited scope; many appeals focus on procedural issues and questions of natural justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing and role of administrative tribunals on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: A tribunal may appear as a party and make representations only as to matters relating to its jurisdiction; it should not debate whether it acted in accordance with principles of natural justice — that issue should be decided by the parties before the reviewing court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court statements (Re Canada Labour Relations Board & Transair) caution tribunals against defending themselves on natural justice grounds on appeal; jurisdictional matters are appropriate for tribunal representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of discrimination/undue preference test to carriers themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of discrimination or undue preference (in relation to tariffs under s.321 Railway Act) applies not only to customers but also to the telephone company relative to its competitors—i.e., a carrier cannot give itself an undue preference in tariffs vis-à-vis competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bell Canada v. Challenge Communications established that tariffs must not unfairly exclude or disadvantage competing suppliers; this extends discrimination analysis to the carrier's competitive conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of service charges as 'telephone tolls' when part of service conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A charge proposed to be levied against customers (e.g., NSF cheque charge) can be part of the total charge for telephone service and therefore classified as a 'telephone toll' requiring filing for approval under the Railway Act when the charge is introduced as a condition of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: B.C. Telephone Company case: Court viewed such charges as contractual conditions of service and therefore within tariff/regulatory approval requirements.
